questions.question: What is the most common site of a traumatic aortic injury in survivors who reach the hospital?
questions.detail: The isthmus is a point of fixation; deceleration causes shear stress at this specific junction.

questions.question: A "Grade III" traumatic aortic injury, according to standard grading, refers to:
questions.detail: Grading typically follows: I (intimal tear), II (IMH), III (pseudoaneurysm), and IV (rupture).

questions.question: Which imaging finding helps differentiate a "ductus diverticulum" (a normal variant) from an acute traumatic pseudoaneurysm?
choices: Smooth margins and obtuse angles with the aorta
questions.detail: A ductus diverticulum is a smooth, developmental bump; a traumatic injury is typically irregular and associated with surrounding hemorrhage.

questions.question: The presence of "displaced intimal calcification" in the setting of trauma is a sign of:
questions.detail: In the setting of trauma, seeing calcifications pushed into the lumen is a marker of an intimal flap.

questions.question: "Chronic traumatic pseudoaneurysm" is typically identified by which feature?
choices: Peripheral calcification of the wall at the isthmus
questions.detail: Survivors of a small traumatic tear may develop a pseudoaneurysm that calcifies over years.
